That approach has been tested by President Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods and repeated rhetorical suggestions about Canadian sovereignty, which Carney has rebuffed even as he avoids direct confrontation, instead pursuing economic diversification through a potential associate membership with the European Union and a prospective trade agreement with India. At this week's UN gatherings, Carney is working to build coalitions on multilateral reform, humanitarian assistance for Palestinians, and ocean protection, an agenda that has helped him maintain unusually strong domestic approval ratings even as many Western leaders face growing public skepticism about international engagement.

items.title: Morocco Votes for a New Parliament After Gen Z Protests and Migration Surge to Ceuta
items.body: Morocco held elections today. People voted for 395 seats in parliament. Nearly 16 million people could vote. Many young people are unhappy. They cannot find jobs, and healthcare and education are not good enough. This is the first election since young people protested last year. There was also a wave of migration to a Spanish city called Ceuta. No single party is expected to win enough seats alone. So different parties will need to work together to choose the next prime minister. Some groups did not want people to vote at all, saying the system is not fair. Results are expected tomorrow.

items.title: Morocco Votes for a New Parliament After Gen Z Protests and Migration Surge to Ceuta
items.body: Morocco held parliamentary elections on Wednesday, with voters choosing representatives for the country's 395-seat legislature. Nearly 16 million citizens were eligible to cast ballots at a time of widespread frustration, especially among young people struggling with unemployment and limited access to healthcare and education. This is the first election since last year's youth-led Gen Z protests and a surge of migration toward the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Since no single party is expected to win an outright majority, coalition talks will likely determine who becomes the next prime minister. Some political groups called for a boycott, arguing the electoral system does not allow for genuine democratic change. Final results are expected on Thursday.

items.title: Morocco Votes for a New Parliament After Gen Z Protests and Migration Surge to Ceuta
items.body: Morocco went to the polls on Wednesday to elect a new 395-seat parliament, in a vote seen as a key test of the political system's ability to respond to the grievances that fueled last year's youth-led protest movement and a related surge in migration attempts toward the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Nearly 16 million citizens were eligible to vote amid persistent frustration over youth unemployment and inadequate access to healthcare and education, issues that dominated the Gen Z demonstrations. With no party projected to win an outright majority, the composition of the next government will likely hinge on post-election coalition negotiations, a process that could take weeks to produce a new prime minister. Several political and civil society groups called for a boycott ahead of the vote, arguing that structural features of the electoral system limit the potential for meaningful change regardless of the outcome, a critique that echoes broader disillusionment among younger Moroccans about whether formal politics can address their concerns. Official results are expected Thursday, though coalition-building is likely to extend well beyond that.

items.title: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell Help Fever Keep Home-Court Hope Alive With 96-77 Win Over Lynx
items.body: In basketball, the Indiana Fever beat the Minnesota Lynx, 96 to 77. Caitlin Clark scored 27 points. She also had 9 assists and 7 rebounds. Her teammate Kelsey Mitchell scored 20 points. Mitchell has now scored 20 or more points in 27 games in a row, a new WNBA record! This win keeps Indiana's small hope of making the playoffs alive. The Lynx played without an injured player named Olivia Miles. Minnesota tried to come back in the second half, but Indiana kept winning.

items.title: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell Help Fever Keep Home-Court Hope Alive With 96-77 Win Over Lynx
items.body: The Indiana Fever defeated the Minnesota Lynx 96-77 in a WNBA game played in Indianapolis, with Caitlin Clark leading Indiana with 27 points, nine assists, and seven rebounds. Teammate Kelsey Mitchell added 20 points of her own, extending her WNBA record to 27 consecutive games with at least 20 points scored. The win keeps alive Indiana's slim chances of securing a playoff spot, with a shot at the fourth seed and home-court advantage still possible. Minnesota played without injured rookie Olivia Miles and rested most of its starters in the second half. Although the Lynx briefly cut the deficit to single digits, the Fever pulled away to secure the victory.

items.title: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell Help Fever Keep Home-Court Hope Alive With 96-77 Win Over Lynx
items.body: Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell combined to lead the Indiana Fever to a 96-77 win over the Minnesota Lynx, with Clark posting 27 points, nine assists, and seven rebounds while Mitchell added 20 points to stretch her WNBA-record streak of 20-plus-point games to 27 in a row. The victory keeps alive Indiana's narrow path to the postseason, with the No. 4 seed and accompanying home-court advantage still mathematically within reach heading into the final stretch of the regular season. Minnesota, already playing without injured rookie Olivia Miles, opted to rest most of its starters for long stretches of the second half, a decision that briefly allowed the Lynx to cut the deficit to single digits before Indiana reasserted control down the stretch. The result underscores both the Fever's late-season resilience and the shifting calculus for a Lynx team already thinking ahead to the playoffs.

items.title: Pakistani Officials Say Afghan Taliban Shelled Pakistani Border. Kabul Denies the Attack
items.body: There was fighting at the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan. Pakistan says Afghan Taliban forces attacked Pakistani border posts. This happened after Pakistan stopped some fighters from crossing the border. Afghanistan's government denies attacking. Before this, Pakistan had bombed places in Afghanistan. Pakistan said it was hitting militant hideouts. But Afghanistan says the bombs hurt regular people too. Pakistan often says Afghanistan lets Pakistani militants live there safely, and these militants attack Pakistan from across the border. Countries like China, Turkey, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia have been trying to help the two sides make peace, but this fighting makes that harder.

items.title: Pakistani Officials Say Afghan Taliban Shelled Pakistani Border. Kabul Denies the Attack
items.body: Pakistani officials say Afghan Taliban forces shelled Pakistani border posts after security forces there stopped an attempted infiltration by militants, an account the Taliban government in Kabul strongly denies. The clash follows recent Pakistani airstrikes on eastern Afghanistan, which Islamabad says targeted militant hideouts but which Kabul says also killed civilians. The exchange ends several weeks of relative calm along the volatile border. Pakistan has long accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing Pakistani militant groups to operate from Afghan territory, using it as a base to carry out attacks inside Pakistan, a claim Kabul rejects. The latest fighting complicates ongoing peace mediation efforts being led by China, Turkey, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, which have been trying to help the two neighbors de-escalate tensions.

items.title: Pakistani Officials Say Afghan Taliban Shelled Pakistani Border. Kabul Denies the Attack
items.body: Pakistani officials say Afghan Taliban forces shelled several Pakistani border posts after security forces repelled an attempted militant infiltration, an account flatly denied by a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kabul, in an exchange that has reignited tensions along one of the region's most volatile frontiers. The clash follows a round of Pakistani airstrikes on eastern Afghanistan that Islamabad said targeted militant hideouts, but which Afghan officials say also killed civilians, ending several weeks of relative calm that had followed earlier rounds of cross-border fighting this year. Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of tacitly allowing Pakistani militant groups, particularly the Pakistani Taliban, to operate from safe havens inside Afghanistan and launch attacks across the border, an allegation Kabul consistently denies while accusing Islamabad of violating Afghan sovereignty with unilateral strikes. The latest flare-up complicates an already difficult regional mediation effort, with China, Turkey, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia all involved in attempts to broker a more durable de-escalation between the two governments, whose relationship has deteriorated sharply over the past year despite decades of historically close ties.

items.title: Final Week of WNBA Regular Season Has Playoff Picture Still Muddled
items.body: The WNBA regular season is almost over. All eight playoff teams are now known. But their playoff positions, called seeds, are not decided yet. Minnesota and Golden State are fighting for the number one seed. This means home-court advantage in the playoffs. In the middle of the standings, many teams are very close. Only two games separate the 4th-place team from the 8th-place team! This week's games between Minnesota and Indiana, and between New York and Atlanta, will help decide the final playoff order. Also, a rookie player named Olivia Miles broke Caitlin Clark's scoring record for first-year players. And Los Angeles built a statue of basketball legend Lisa Leslie outside their arena.

items.title: Final Week of WNBA Regular Season Has Playoff Picture Still Muddled
items.body: As the WNBA regular season enters its final week, the eight teams that will make the playoffs have already been determined, but their exact seeding remains unsettled. Minnesota and Golden State are locked in a tight battle for the top seed and the home-court advantage that comes with it, while the middle and lower playoff positions are separated by just two games between fourth place and eighth place. Key matchups this week, including games between Minnesota and Indiana and between New York and Atlanta, are expected to play a significant role in shaping the final playoff bracket. Off the court, rookie Olivia Miles broke Caitlin Clark's rookie scoring record, and the Los Angeles franchise unveiled a statue honoring basketball legend Lisa Leslie outside its arena.

items.title: Final Week of WNBA Regular Season Has Playoff Picture Still Muddled
items.body: With the WNBA regular season heading into its final week, the identities of the eight playoff qualifiers have already been settled, but the seeding that will shape the entire postseason bracket remains unusually competitive. Minnesota and Golden State remain locked in a close race for the No. 1 seed and the home-court advantage it confers, while the gap separating fourth place from eighth place has narrowed to just two games, setting up a chaotic final stretch across the middle of the standings. This week's schedule, headlined by matchups between Minnesota and Indiana and between New York and Atlanta, is expected to go a long way toward determining the final playoff order before the postseason begins. Beyond the standings race, the league also marked several notable milestones this week: rookie Olivia Miles surpassed Caitlin Clark's rookie-season scoring record, while the Los Angeles franchise unveiled a statue honoring WNBA pioneer Lisa Leslie outside its home arena, underscoring the growing visibility and investment surrounding the league heading into an increasingly competitive postseason.

items.title: A Timeline of US President Donald Trump's Interest in Greenland
items.body: President Trump has wanted to buy Greenland since 2019. Greenland belongs to Denmark. At first, people thought this idea was strange. But Trump brought it back during his second term as president. Between late 2024 and 2026, Trump used strong words and threatened taxes, called tariffs, on European countries to pressure Denmark. Denmark and Greenland both said no. Greenland's leaders said they would rather stay with Denmark than join the US. Early in 2026, Trump threatened even more pressure, but later he backed down. Finally, in September 2026, the two sides made a security agreement. Denmark keeps control of Greenland, but the US gets to use more military bases there. Trump did not say clearly if he still wants to buy the island.

items.title: A Timeline of US President Donald Trump's Interest in Greenland
items.body: President Trump's interest in acquiring Greenland, a Danish territory, dates back to 2019, when the idea was largely dismissed as unrealistic. It resurfaced more seriously during his second term, escalating between late 2024 and 2026 through a mix of military rhetoric and economic pressure, including threatened tariffs against European countries. Denmark and Greenland consistently rejected the proposal, with Greenlandic leaders making clear they would prefer to remain part of Denmark rather than come under US control. Tensions peaked in early 2026 when Trump threatened further punitive measures, though these were eventually withdrawn. By September 2026, the dispute was resolved, at least for now, through a security agreement that preserves Danish sovereignty over Greenland while significantly expanding the US military presence on the island. Notably, Trump has stopped short of confirming whether he has given up his broader ambitions to acquire the territory outright.

items.title: A Timeline of US President Donald Trump's Interest in Greenland
items.body: President Trump's on-and-off pursuit of Greenland traces back to 2019, when his first-term suggestion that the US might purchase the Danish territory was widely mocked as implausible. The idea returned with far greater intensity during his second term, escalating between late 2024 and 2026 through a combination of military rhetoric and economic coercion, including repeated threats of tariffs against Denmark and other European nations. Throughout, both Copenhagen and Nuuk firmly rejected any suggestion of a transfer of sovereignty, with Greenlandic leaders stating unambiguously that they would rather remain part of the Danish realm than fall under American control. The standoff reached its most acute point in early 2026, when Trump threatened additional punitive measures against Denmark, before ultimately backing away from that escalation. By September 2026, the dispute had been at least provisionally resolved through a security agreement that formally preserves Danish sovereignty over Greenland while substantially expanding the US military footprint on the island, reflecting Washington's underlying strategic interest in the territory's location and resources. Trump, notably, has stopped short of stating whether his original ambition to acquire Greenland outright has been abandoned or merely deferred, leaving open the possibility that the issue could resurface.

items.title: Leite Has Big Baskets in Overtime as the Fire End the Season With a 90-82 Win Over the Valkyries
items.body: In basketball, the Portland Fire beat the Golden State Valkyries, 90 to 82. The game went into overtime, extra playing time. Gabby Williams scored 17 points for Golden State. Golden State started the game very well, leading 17-0 at first. But they could not keep the lead. This loss ended Golden State's six-game winning streak. It also means the Minnesota Lynx will get the number one playoff seed. Portland's win ended their own four-game losing streak.

items.title: Leite Has Big Baskets in Overtime as the Fire End the Season With a 90-82 Win Over the Valkyries
items.body: The Portland Fire edged the Golden State Valkyries 90-82 in overtime to close out their WNBA regular season. Carla Leite proved to be the difference-maker in the extra period, hitting the go-ahead shot with under two minutes left and later adding a clutch three-point play. Bridget Carleton led Portland with 26 points, while Gabby Williams topped Golden State with 17. The Valkyries had jumped out to an early 17-0 lead but were unable to hold on. The defeat snapped Golden State's six-game winning streak and, as a result, mathematically locked in the Minnesota Lynx as the league's No. 1 playoff seed. For Portland, the win ended a four-game losing streak, while Golden State has just one game left in the regular season, against Los Angeles.

items.title: Leite Has Big Baskets in Overtime as the Fire End the Season With a 90-82 Win Over the Valkyries
items.body: The Portland Fire closed out their regular season with a 90-82 overtime win over the Golden State Valkyries, a result that also had significant playoff implications elsewhere in the standings. Carla Leite was decisive in the extra period, hitting the go-ahead basket with under two minutes remaining and later sealing the win with a clutch three-point play, while Bridget Carleton finished with a game-high 26 points for Portland and Gabby Williams led Golden State with 17. The Valkyries raced out to an early 17-0 lead but were unable to sustain their dominance as Portland steadily clawed back and eventually forced overtime. The loss snapped Golden State's six-game winning streak and, combined with results elsewhere, mathematically secured the Minnesota Lynx the league's No. 1 seed heading into the playoffs. For Portland, the win offered a measure of redemption, ending a four-game losing streak on a high note, while Golden State has just one regular-season game remaining, against Los Angeles, before turning its attention to the postseason.

items.title: Your body language may shape who you are
items.summary: Social psychologist Amy Cuddy explains how nonverbal cues do more than signal confidence to others - holding an expansive, high-power posture for a couple of minutes before a stressful situation, she argues, can change how confident we feel inside. She frames this as "fake it until you become it" rather than just faking it to impress people. Note: later replication studies questioned the hormonal effects she originally cited, so the talk is best read as a popular case for confident body language rather than settled science.

items.title: One of the most banned books of all time
items.summary: Education scholar Mollie Godfrey examines why Maya Angelou's memoir "I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings" has been one of the most frequently banned books in American schools since a 1998 controversy, when a school district pulled it over objections that it was sexually explicit and anti-white. She traces the memoir's unflinching account of racism and childhood sexual abuse and argues for why that same content makes it an important, widely taught work.

items.title: How porn changes the way teens think about sex
items.summary: Public health researcher Emily Rothman argues that because comprehensive sex education is often missing or inadequate, mainstream online pornography has effectively become many teenagers' default source of information about sex - one that skews their expectations. She describes the pornography-literacy curriculum she developed, which teaches teens to critically analyze what they see online and understand consent, rather than simply telling them not to watch.

items.title: A whale's-eye-view of the ocean
items.summary: Engineer Eric Stackpole tells the story of building a low-cost, suction-cup camera rig that captured rare footage of two sperm whales swimming and apparently communicating in the deep ocean, a scene no one had filmed before. He uses the project as a case for democratized exploration - arguing that scrappy, homemade tools built by curious amateurs can still reveal things about the ocean that expensive institutional research hasn't caught.

items.title: How to reclaim your life from work
items.summary: Writer Simone Stolzoff questions the modern habit of building one's entire identity around a job, describing how that "workism" leaves people vulnerable when a career stumbles or ends. Drawing on interviews with workers who redefined their relationship to their jobs, he lays out practical ways to separate self-worth from professional output and reclaim time and meaning outside the office.

items.title: Exploring the mind of a killer
items.summary: Neuroscientist Jim Fallon describes patterns he has found in brain scans and genetics that correlate with psychopathic and violent behavior, then reveals an unsettling twist: while studying murderers' brain scans anonymously for comparison, he found one scan matching the psychopathic pattern he was researching - and it turned out to be his own. He uses his family's history to explore how genetics ("nature") interacts with upbringing ("nurture") in producing violence.

items.title: The real story of McMafia -- how global crime networks work
items.summary: Journalist Misha Glenny recounts years spent investigating organized crime networks - drug cartels, human traffickers, arms dealers and cybercriminals - that he estimates now account for roughly 15 percent of the global economy. Drawing on firsthand interviews with mobsters and criminals across multiple countries, he explains how globalization and the internet have let organized crime operate as an efficient, borderless business.

items.title: I thought I was lazy. Turns out I had a sleep disorder
items.summary: Sleep health educator Lindsay Scola spent over twenty years blaming her constant exhaustion on long hours and a demanding career, until a diagnosis of narcolepsy forced her to rethink it. She uses her own story to highlight how common undiagnosed sleep disorders are, and urges listeners who feel chronically "lazy" or tired to consider whether something medical, not just workload, might explain it.

items.title: Salvation (and profit) in greentech
items.summary: Venture capitalist John Doerr makes an emotional case that current efforts to fight climate change are falling far short, framing the crisis in terms of the world he wants to leave his daughter. He argues that solving it requires treating clean energy as a serious investment opportunity, not just an environmental cause, and calls on entrepreneurs and financiers to pour resources into scaling greentech the way earlier generations funded the internet and biotech.

items.title: The political chemistry of oil
items.summary: Speaking a month after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, journalist Lisa Margonelli argues that public outrage over spill cleanups and executive firings misses the real problem: everyday consumer demand for cheap oil. She proposes confronting drivers with the full, hidden cost of oil at the pump, rather than treating disasters as isolated events, as the more honest way to actually reduce consumption.
